mcq.q:
Consider the following statements about colonial India:
1. V.K.R.V. Rao's estimates of national income were considered very significant.
2. The colonial government made a sincere attempt to estimate India's national income.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
mcq.why: NCERT: the colonial government never made any sincere attempt; among individual estimators, Rao's estimates were considered very significant.

mcq.q: Arrange these events in chronological order (earliest first), using NCERT's dates:
options: Suez Canal opens, first census, TISCO, Tata Airlines
First census, Suez Canal opens, TISCO, Tata Airlines
Suez Canal opens, TISCO, first census, Tata Airlines
First census, TISCO, Suez Canal opens, Tata Airlines
mcq.why: Suez Canal 1869, first census 1881, TISCO 1907, Tata Airlines 1932. (Suez: foreign-trade reel; census: demographic-transition reel.)

mcq.q: According to NCERT's occupational structure of colonial India, the agricultural sector's share of the workforce was usually:
mcq.why: Section 1.7: agriculture's share of the workforce stayed at a high of 70–75%. (Separately, about 85% of the population lived in villages and depended on agriculture: don't mix the two figures.)

mcq.q:
Consider the following statements about early modern industry in India:
1. Jute mills were mainly located in the western parts of the country.
2. Cotton textile mills were mainly dominated by Indians.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
mcq.why: Cotton textile mills, mainly dominated by Indians, were in western India (Maharashtra, Gujarat); jute mills, dominated by foreigners, were mainly concentrated in Bengal.

mcq.q: Which of the following is correctly matched for India around independence, as per NCERT?
mcq.why: NCERT: IMR about 218 per thousand, life expectancy about 32 years, overall literacy below 16%, female literacy about 7%.

mcq.q:
According to NCERT, consider the following statements about India's export surplus during colonial rule:
1. It brought large inflows of gold and silver into India.
2. It was used to pay for the expenses of an office set up by the colonial government in Britain.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
mcq.why: NCERT: 'this export surplus did not result in any flow of gold or silver into India'. It paid for the colonial office in Britain, for wars fought by the British government and for invisible imports: the drain of Indian wealth.

mcq.q: Which of the following was NOT a purpose of colonial infrastructure according to NCERT?
options: Carrying raw materials to the ports
Maintaining law and order by telegraph
Providing basic amenities to the people
mcq.why: NCERT: the real motive was to serve colonial interests (army movement, raw materials to ports, law and order), not to provide basic amenities to the people.

mcq.q: The Madras Presidency of colonial India comprised areas of which present-day states?
options: Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh, Kerala and Karnataka
Gujarat, Maharashtra, Goa and coastal Karnataka
Odisha, West Bengal, Bihar and parts of Assam
Punjab, Haryana, Rajasthan and western Delhi
mcq.why: NCERT, section 1.7: the Madras Presidency comprised areas of present-day Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh, Kerala and Karnataka.

mcq.q:
Consider the following statements about the zamindari system:
1. Under it, the profit from agriculture went to the zamindars instead of the cultivators.
2. The terms of revenue settlement fixed dates for depositing revenue, failing which zamindars lost their rights.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
mcq.why: Both are NCERT points: profits went to zamindars, and the revenue settlement's fixed dates made zamindars squeeze cultivators.

mcq.q: In NCERT's terms, a capital goods industry is one that:
options: Produces machine tools used to make articles for consumption
Produces luxury goods mainly for export to rich nations
Is owned and financed entirely by the colonial government
Produces food grains and raw materials for British mills
mcq.why: Capital goods industries produce machine tools, which are in turn used to produce articles for current consumption.

mcq.q: During colonial rule, the public sector's area of operation was confined mainly to:
options: Railways, power generation, communications and ports
Iron and steel, cement, sugar and paper mills
Cotton textiles, jute mills and handicrafts
mcq.why: NCERT: the public sector was confined to railways, power generation, communications, ports and some departmental undertakings.

mcq.q: Apart from Britain, which countries does NCERT name as India's trading partners under colonial rule?
options: USA, Germany and the Soviet Union
mcq.why: More than half of India's foreign trade was restricted to Britain; the rest was allowed with a few countries like China, Ceylon and Persia.

mcq.q:
Consider the following statements about India's demographic transition (NCERT):
1. Before 1921, India was in the first stage of demographic transition.
2. The second stage of demographic transition began after 1947.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
mcq.why: NCERT: before 1921 India was in the first stage; the second stage began after 1921 (not 1947).

mcq.q: Who among the following is NOT named by NCERT as an estimator of India's national income during the colonial period?
mcq.why: The estimators: Dadabhai Naoroji, William Digby, Findlay Shirras, V.K.R.V. Rao and R.C. Desai. R.C. Dutt wrote 'Economic History of India'; don't confuse him with Desai.

mcq.q: According to NCERT's opening quote, who was the Viceroy of British India who in 1894 called India 'the pivot of our Empire'?
mcq.why: NCERT quotes the Viceroy of British India in 1894, printed as 'Victor Alexander Vruce', i.e. Victor Alexander Bruce, Lord Elgin.

mcq.q: According to NCERT, about what share of India's population lived in villages and depended on agriculture under colonial rule?
mcq.why: About 85% lived in villages and depended on agriculture directly or indirectly. (Agriculture's share of the workforce was 70–75%.)

mcq.q: The Coast Canal, built at huge cost but abandoned because a parallel railway out-competed it, was on the coast of:
mcq.why: NCERT: the Coast Canal on the Orissa coast failed to compete with the railways running parallel to it and had to be abandoned.

mcq.q:
Consider the following statements about colonial India's high mortality (NCERT):
1. Water-borne and air-borne diseases were rampant.
2. Frequent natural calamities and famines pauperised the people.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
mcq.why: Both are NCERT causes, along with unavailable or inadequate public health facilities.

descriptive.q: What was the focus of the economic policies pursued by the colonial government in India? What were the impacts of these policies?
keyPoints: Focus: concerned more with protecting and promoting Britain's economic interests than with developing the Indian economy
India turned into a supplier of raw materials for British industry
And a consumer (market) for Britain's finished goods
Impacts: de-industrialisation and decline of handicrafts
Agricultural stagnation and low growth (under 2% aggregate, about 0.5% per capita)
Drain of wealth through the export surplus

descriptive.q: What were the main causes of India's agricultural stagnation during the colonial period?
keyPoints: Land settlement systems, especially zamindari: profits went to zamindars
A considerable number of zamindars, and not just the colonial government, did nothing to improve agriculture
Zamindars only collected rent; revenue settlement terms (fixed dates) made them harsh
Low technology
Lack of irrigation facilities
Negligible use of fertilisers
Despite some irrigation progress, starved of investment in terracing, flood-control, drainage and desalinisation of soil
Commercialisation: cash crops served British industry; tenants, small farmers and sharecroppers lacked resources, technology and incentive to invest

descriptive.q: What was the two-fold motive behind the systematic de-industrialisation effected by the British in pre-independent India?
keyPoints: Reduce India to an exporter of important raw materials for Britain's modern industries
Turn India into a sprawling market for Britain's finished products
So British industry could expand to Britain's maximum advantage

descriptive.q: The traditional handicrafts industries were ruined under British rule. Do you agree with this view? Give reasons in support of your answer.
keyPoints: Agree: India was famous for handicrafts (cotton and silk textiles, metal and precious stone work, Dhaka muslin)
Policy aimed at de-industrialisation for Britain's benefit
Handicrafts declined with no modern industry to replace them
Massive unemployment among artisans
Demand met by cheap British imports

descriptive.q: What objectives did the British intend to achieve through their policies of infrastructure development in India?
keyPoints: Serve colonial interests, not provide basic amenities to the people
Roads mobilised the army within India
Roads drew raw materials from the countryside to the nearest railway station or port, for export to England and other destinations
The expensive electric telegraph served to maintain law and order
Efforts were made, but they were 'spiced with selfish motives' (Recap)

descriptive.q: Critically appraise some of the shortfalls of the industrial policy pursued by the British colonial administration.
keyPoints: Systematic de-industrialisation; handicrafts not replaced by modern industry
Hardly any capital goods industry
Very slow growth of modern industry, mostly cotton and jute
Industrial sector's growth rate and share of GDP/GVA very small
Public sector very limited (railways, power, communications, ports)

descriptive.q: What do you understand by the drain of Indian wealth during the colonial period?
keyPoints: India had a large export surplus
It brought no gold or silver into India
It paid for an office set up by the colonial government in Britain
And for wars fought by the British government and imports of invisible items
Essentials (food grains, clothes, kerosene) were scarce at home

descriptive.q: Give a quantitative appraisal of India's demographic profile during the colonial period.
keyPoints: First census 1881 (it revealed uneven population growth); census every 10 years after
Before 1921, first stage of demographic transition; second stage after 1921
Neither the total population nor its growth rate was very high at this stage
Overall literacy below 16%, female literacy about 7%
Infant mortality about 218 per thousand; life expectancy about 32 years
High mortality (inadequate public health, water- and air-borne diseases); extensive poverty

descriptive.q: Highlight the salient features of India's pre-independence occupational structure.
keyPoints: Little sign of change
Agriculture 70–75% of the workforce
Manufacturing about 10%, services 15–20%
Growing regional variation
Madras, Bombay, Bengal: less dependence on agriculture; Orissa, Rajasthan, Punjab: more

descriptive.q: Underscore some of India's most crucial economic challenges at the time of independence.
keyPoints: Agriculture: surplus labour and extremely low productivity
Industry: needed modernisation, diversification, capacity building and public investment
Foreign trade oriented to feed Britain's Industrial Revolution
Infrastructure needed upgrading, expansion and public orientation
Rampant poverty and unemployment needed welfare-oriented policy

descriptive.q: Indicate the volume and direction of trade at the time of independence.
keyPoints: Volume: a large export surplus, at a huge cost to the economy; restrictive colonial policies on commodity production, trade and tariffs hurt trade
Composition: exporter of primary products, importer of finished consumer goods and light machinery
Direction: Britain kept monopoly control over exports and imports; more than half of trade restricted to Britain
The rest with a few countries such as China, Ceylon and Persia
Suez Canal (1869) intensified British control

descriptive.q: Were there any positive contributions made by the British in India? Discuss.
keyPoints: Some positives: railways (long-distance travel, broke geographical and cultural barriers), roads, ports, telegraph, posts
But their real motive was to serve colonial interests, not to provide amenities
Railways fostered commercialisation of agriculture, hurting village self-sufficiency; social benefits outweighed by huge economic loss
Costs: drain of wealth, de-industrialisation, agricultural stagnation
Conclusion: infrastructure efforts were made, but they were 'spiced with selfish motives'
